items.question: explain this like a story
items.script:
say A linear combination is finding the right mix of directions to reach a goal.
say Sam wants to reach a treasure hidden at this specific spot on his map.
note 535 235 60 135 | The Treasure | Target destination Sam must reach
say He tries walking but can only follow these two slanted paths.
note 265 235 200 135 | Allowed Paths | Sam's only two directions of travel
say Aha! By mixing the two paths, he lands right on the treasure.
say It's called a linear combination, but real vectors can work in any dimension.
title Vector path story

items.question: show me step by step how to solve this
items.script:
say The solution is x equals 1 and y equals 2.
say Think of this as mixing two ingredients to hit a target.
step 1 420 260 | 2x - y = 0
say Row one says y must be twice x to balance to zero.
step 2 420 340 | -x + 2y = 3
say Row two then forces x to be 1, and it all checks out.
ring 260 220 340 160 | x=1, y=2
title Solving the column picture

items.question: how would they test this, exam style?
items.script:

ring 535 235 60 135 | target | The goal

choices Yes, give me one | Not now

items.question: what is a matrix?
items.script:
say A matrix is a grid of numbers that acts like a vector's instruction manual.
say Picture Sam's robot: it has a messy pile of movement instructions.
say He tries a long list, but packs them into this grid box instead.
note 265 235 200 135 | The Matrix | A grid of rules for vectors
say Aha! It's a linear transformation, though real ones can be massive.
title What is a matrix?

items.question: why do we write it as a matrix?
items.script:
say A matrix keeps giant systems of equations compact and easy to handle.
say Sam's robot has way too many legs to track them all separately.
note 265 235 200 135 | Matrix | Sam's grid for managing robot leg instructions
say Aha! Packing them into a grid lets him move them all together.
say It's matrix notation, but real robots can't always move in straight lines.
title Why use matrices?

items.question: what does the x mean here?
items.script:
say x is the amount or "weight" of the first direction you take.
say Picture Sam's map: x tells him exactly how many steps to walk on path one.
note 265 240 25 35 | x | The number of steps on path one
say Aha! By scaling path one by x, he gets closer to the goal.
say It's called a scalar, but real paths aren't always perfectly straight.
title What is x?

items.question: what is a system of linear equations?
items.script:
say A system of linear equations is a set of rules that must all be true.
say Sam is looking for a meeting point where two straight paths cross each other.
note 260 230 350 145 | The System | Multiple rules that must work together
say Aha! The spot where both paths meet is the only solution.
say This is a linear system, but real-world curves aren't always straight lines.
title Systems of linear equations

items.question: explain this diagram
items.script:
say This is a neural network "brain" recognizing the handwritten number 2.
ring 35 115 110 195 | input image | The handwritten digit Sam wrote
say Look at the right side. When the network sees this shape, the neuron for 2 glows brightest.
ring 510 330 25 35 | output 2 | The network's final guess
say Information flows through layers, where each circle is a "neuron" that votes on the next step.
title How neural networks recognize digits

items.question: what are these circles?
items.script:
say These circles are "neurons" that hold a number representing how much they're "glowing."
ring 345 440 25 35 | neuron | One small processor
say Look at one neuron. It glows bright when it spots a specific pattern in the layer before it.
arrow 300 440 -> 345 440 | connection
say Each glowing neuron passes its strength along these lines to influence the next layer.
title What is a neuron?

items.question: what do the lines between them mean?
items.script:
say They are like volume knobs, called weights, that show how much one neuron influences another.
note 343 150 89 560 | Weights | Connection strength
say Look at the bright yellow lines: they show a very strong connection.
ring 388 425 70 | strong weights
say If you dim a line, that specific connection becomes weaker and less important.
arrow 343 425 -> 432 425 | influence
say The math multiplies the neuron's brightness by this weight to pass signal on.
title Neural network weights

items.question: how does a neural network learn?
items.script:
say It learns by adjusting its "volume knobs" to get more answers right.
say Imagine a voter who shouts "five" at a picture of a "two."
note 511 430 30 30 | Oops! | Shouting the wrong number
say We nudge every dial until the "two" neuron glows the brightest.
note 511 325 30 30 | Aha! | Finally getting it right
say This is "backpropagation," but real brain cells don't use this specific math.
title How neural networks learn

items.question: explain this like a story
items.script:
say It is a team of specialists finding shapes in a mess.
say Dot the detective sees a squiggle and wonders if it's a squashed bug.
note 35 120 100 180 | The Problem | Messy pixels
say He asks friends to find edges, then loops, until they build the number.
note 330 150 150 560 | Feature Extraction | Finding shapes step by step
say "Aha! It's a two!" This story breaks because networks only see math, not meanings.
title Feature detection story
